items.title: Macmillan Staff Say the Publisher Threw a Party for a Workplace AI Assistant That Was Later Killed
items.title_en: Macmillan Staff Say the Publisher Threw a Party for a Workplace AI Assistant That Was Later Killed
items.author: Wired AI
items.article_content:
As staff at the Lower Manhattan headquarters of Macmillan Publishers headed into work one morning in January 2024, they filed past something strange on the walls—flyers welcoming a new member of the team named “NOA.” The cafeteria was festooned with purple balloons and banners, according to several workers present, and with NOA’s name in light-up marquee letters. A plate full of doughnuts spelled out “NOA IS HERE.”

NOA was an acronym for No Ordinary Assistant, which many of Macmillan’s human assistants found “offensive,” multiple employees tell WIRED. In an email to staff, NOA was introduced as an AI chatbot developed by the German software company Chaptr, which is “backed” by Holtzbrinck, Macmillan’s parent company.

The email also assured employees NOA was “a safe environment where you can input proprietary information without the risk of sharing that data with any third party.” Ostensibly, this means NOA was a closed-loop enterprise tool that did not retain or share data for model training.

Macmillan staffers say they were warned during training sessions that NOA could hallucinate and would always need to be fact-checked by humans. Still, employees say, they were encouraged to use NOA for composing emails, drafting copy, doing marketing research, and generating ideas. Multiple staffers say they were told to “only” paste a “percentage” of authors’ manuscripts into NOA. Employees could also adjust NOA’s speaking tone, with options including “lighthearted,” “spartan,” pessimistic,” “sarcastic,” and “regretful.”

One Macmillan employee remembers a Chaptr representative reassuring workers during an early in-person training session that Chaptr understood publishers were dealing with something very important—content. “And here I thought we were publishing literature,” the employee says.

Later in 2024, Macmillan employees were encouraged to use NOA to generate their goals for performance reviews. “We built a specialized prompt to have NOA write goals for you!” one email read.

Several Macmillan employees say NOA was unhelpful and unreliable. “It was terrible, and no one used it,” one says. WIRED spoke with multiple publishing employees for this article, including some who have since left their employers. WIRED is not naming these employees, nor the authors we interviewed, because they are concerned about professional repercussions.

In October 2025, Macmillan staff learned via a company-wide email that Chaptr would be sunsetting NOA. Since then, workers say, leadership has been attempting to integrate Google Gemini into the publishing process. Some staffers subsequently experimented with using Gemini to evaluate submission letters from literary agents, but the Gemini-generated evaluations were “useless,” according to one editor.

In response to WIRED’s request for comment, Kelly Collins, vice president of communications and community at Macmillan, says the publishing house uses Gemini for its “business” but “there has not been any directive from Macmillan leadership to use Gemini for any part of the publishing process, including to evaluate submission letters from agents.” She also says “the points shared do not accurately reflect how NOA was rolled out and communicated” but did not provide further elaboration when WIRED asked which aspects were inaccurate.

Collins notes that the company “takes a thoughtful approach to AI, focused on employee awareness and education while always keeping people front and center.”

Macmillan is usually cited as the smallest of the Big Five US book publishers based on the number of books sold each year. Its imprint Farrar, Straus and Giroux publishes literary fiction heavyweights like Sally Rooney, Yiyun Li, and Ben Lerner while Tor Books is a home for science fiction and fantasy authors John Scalzi, Martha Wells, and Nnedi Okorafor.

At the same time, multiple bestselling Big Five authors say they’ve gone to “war” with their publishers over AI and are considering abandoning traditional publishing altogether.

In February, representatives from Hay House—a new-age self-help publisher acquired by Penguin Random House in 2023—presented a slide deck to some PRH employees about how ChatGPT Enterprise had become a “core productivity, creativity, and collaboration tool” since they adopted it a year prior. One of the four return-on-investment pillars in the deck was “Creativity,” including “idea generation, content development, and storytelling innovations.”

Despite encouragement from the C-suite, all of the PRH workers WIRED spoke with say they’re avoiding ChatGPT whenever possible. “It makes it harder for us to do our jobs,” one employee says. Other staff say their managers have explicitly asked them not to use AI for creative tasks like publicity copy and cover design, which has caused some confusion.

“Penguin Random House approaches AI as we would any significant new technology,” says Claire von Schilling, executive vice president and director of corporate communications and social responsibility for the publisher, via email. “We are exploring ways it may appropriately support our work, guided by clear principles and safeguards, including protecting the intellectual property of our authors and the company and preserving the essential role of human creativity and judgment in publishing.”

Von Schilling also says that PRH’s “publishing groups and imprints have discretion to determine whether and how AI tools may be appropriate for particular workflows, including areas such as marketing, publicity, and design.”

Meanwhile, several bestselling Big Five authors say their relationships with publishers have suffered over the past year due to AI use. Combined, the Big Five authors WIRED spoke with have sold more than 30 million copies. One bestselling author says they received marketing copy that included AI-hallucinated quotes from their book, but the publisher insisted they were not AI-generated. “I was gaslit on all of it,” the author says. During a recent round of contract negotiations, another bestselling author says they could not get a single Big Five publisher to promise no AI would be used in any way on their books.

“It’s undermining the necessary sense of trust that has to exist between writers and publishers,” one author says.

“It’s also frustrating to watch publishers get these massive settlements [from] AI companies and then embrace AI to do their work,” another author says. “It feels like they’re feeding at both sides of the trough.”

Authors say cost-cutting layoffs at the Big Five have contributed to deteriorating conditions for their editors and forced some to embrace AI for survival. “We’re seeing editors not reading the material at all and using Claude to create marketing language that barely has any relation to the book,” one author says. Other authors and agents say they’ve been asked by editors to write their own plans for revisions “because the editors don’t have time to do it themselves.”

All of the authors I spoke with say they want publishers to communicate when and how they’re using AI. “The bare minimum we're asking for is disclosure,” one author says. Another wishes the Big Five “would get together and come up with a set of principles around AI that they intend to adhere to.” But some bestselling authors say their publishers’ use of AI is forcing them to consider publishing future books on their own.

“What are authors even doing with traditional publishers anymore if they’re going to outsource everything to a machine?” one bestselling author says. “Why can't an author do that themselves?”

Following WIRED's previous reporting, several high-profile authors condemned the adoption of AI tools in publishing. “I have never looked down on other publishing models (zine girly from way back) & every day, self pub looking ever more possible for future work,” Mo Ryan wrote on Bluesky. Her most recent book, Burn It Down: Power, Complicity, and a Call for Change in Hollywood, was published by HarperCollins.

John Scalzi, the sci-fi novelist who signed a 10-book deal with Macmillan’s Tor Publishing Group in 2024, wrote, “I would be EXTREMELY annoyed to discover my PR is ‘AI’-generated, and as someone bombarded with dozens of ‘AI’-generated emails daily, I assure you the stink of ‘AI’ is immediately noticable [sic] and immediately dismissible. Publishers are not doing their new books any favors in using it.”

Bestselling authors who have already accumulated huge readerships say they don’t need the institutional support of a Big Five publisher to sell copies. Brandon Sanderson, for instance, publishes some of his fantasy novels through Tor Books, an imprint of Macmillan, but raised more than $15 million from his readers on Kickstarter to publish four books on his own in 2022.

“Publishers have always seen authors as a bit of a nuisance, and now there’s a desire to make us obsolete,” says one bestselling Big Five author. “What’s fascinating to me is that in the process of trying to make authors obsolete by using AI, the publishers are rendering themselves obsolete.”
items.original_content:
As staff at the Lower Manhattan headquarters of Macmillan Publishers headed into work one morning in January 2024, they filed past something strange on the walls—flyers welcoming a new member of the team named “NOA.” The cafeteria was festooned with purple balloons and banners, according to several workers present, and with NOA’s name in light-up marquee letters. A plate full of doughnuts spelled out “NOA IS HERE.”

NOA was an acronym for No Ordinary Assistant, which many of Macmillan’s human assistants found “offensive,” multiple employees tell WIRED. In an email to staff, NOA was introduced as an AI chatbot developed by the German software company Chaptr, which is “backed” by Holtzbrinck, Macmillan’s parent company.

The email also assured employees NOA was “a safe environment where you can input proprietary information without the risk of sharing that data with any third party.” Ostensibly, this means NOA was a closed-loop enterprise tool that did not retain or share data for model training.

Macmillan staffers say they were warned during training sessions that NOA could hallucinate and would always need to be fact-checked by humans. Still, employees say, they were encouraged to use NOA for composing emails, drafting copy, doing marketing research, and generating ideas. Multiple staffers say they were told to “only” paste a “percentage” of authors’ manuscripts into NOA. Employees could also adjust NOA’s speaking tone, with options including “lighthearted,” “spartan,” pessimistic,” “sarcastic,” and “regretful.”

One Macmillan employee remembers a Chaptr representative reassuring workers during an early in-person training session that Chaptr understood publishers were dealing with something very important—content. “And here I thought we were publishing literature,” the employee says.

Later in 2024, Macmillan employees were encouraged to use NOA to generate their goals for performance reviews. “We built a specialized prompt to have NOA write goals for you!” one email read.

Several Macmillan employees say NOA was unhelpful and unreliable. “It was terrible, and no one used it,” one says. WIRED spoke with multiple publishing employees for this article, including some who have since left their employers. WIRED is not naming these employees, nor the authors we interviewed, because they are concerned about professional repercussions.

In October 2025, Macmillan staff learned via a company-wide email that Chaptr would be sunsetting NOA. Since then, workers say, leadership has been attempting to integrate Google Gemini into the publishing process. Some staffers subsequently experimented with using Gemini to evaluate submission letters from literary agents, but the Gemini-generated evaluations were “useless,” according to one editor.

In response to WIRED’s request for comment, Kelly Collins, vice president of communications and community at Macmillan, says the publishing house uses Gemini for its “business” but “there has not been any directive from Macmillan leadership to use Gemini for any part of the publishing process, including to evaluate submission letters from agents.” She also says “the points shared do not accurately reflect how NOA was rolled out and communicated” but did not provide further elaboration when WIRED asked which aspects were inaccurate.

Collins notes that the company “takes a thoughtful approach to AI, focused on employee awareness and education while always keeping people front and center.”

Macmillan is usually cited as the smallest of the Big Five US book publishers based on the number of books sold each year. Its imprint Farrar, Straus and Giroux publishes literary fiction heavyweights like Sally Rooney, Yiyun Li, and Ben Lerner while Tor Books is a home for science fiction and fantasy authors John Scalzi, Martha Wells, and Nnedi Okorafor.

At the same time, multiple bestselling Big Five authors say they’ve gone to “war” with their publishers over AI and are considering abandoning traditional publishing altogether.

In February, representatives from Hay House—a new-age self-help publisher acquired by Penguin Random House in 2023—presented a slide deck to some PRH employees about how ChatGPT Enterprise had become a “core productivity, creativity, and collaboration tool” since they adopted it a year prior. One of the four return-on-investment pillars in the deck was “Creativity,” including “idea generation, content development, and storytelling innovations.”

Despite encouragement from the C-suite, all of the PRH workers WIRED spoke with say they’re avoiding ChatGPT whenever possible. “It makes it harder for us to do our jobs,” one employee says. Other staff say their managers have explicitly asked them not to use AI for creative tasks like publicity copy and cover design, which has caused some confusion.

“Penguin Random House approaches AI as we would any significant new technology,” says Claire von Schilling, executive vice president and director of corporate communications and social responsibility for the publisher, via email. “We are exploring ways it may appropriately support our work, guided by clear principles and safeguards, including protecting the intellectual property of our authors and the company and preserving the essential role of human creativity and judgment in publishing.”

Von Schilling also says that PRH’s “publishing groups and imprints have discretion to determine whether and how AI tools may be appropriate for particular workflows, including areas such as marketing, publicity, and design.”

Meanwhile, several bestselling Big Five authors say their relationships with publishers have suffered over the past year due to AI use. Combined, the Big Five authors WIRED spoke with have sold more than 30 million copies. One bestselling author says they received marketing copy that included AI-hallucinated quotes from their book, but the publisher insisted they were not AI-generated. “I was gaslit on all of it,” the author says. During a recent round of contract negotiations, another bestselling author says they could not get a single Big Five publisher to promise no AI would be used in any way on their books.

“It’s undermining the necessary sense of trust that has to exist between writers and publishers,” one author says.

“It’s also frustrating to watch publishers get these massive settlements [from] AI companies and then embrace AI to do their work,” another author says. “It feels like they’re feeding at both sides of the trough.”

Authors say cost-cutting layoffs at the Big Five have contributed to deteriorating conditions for their editors and forced some to embrace AI for survival. “We’re seeing editors not reading the material at all and using Claude to create marketing language that barely has any relation to the book,” one author says. Other authors and agents say they’ve been asked by editors to write their own plans for revisions “because the editors don’t have time to do it themselves.”

All of the authors I spoke with say they want publishers to communicate when and how they’re using AI. “The bare minimum we're asking for is disclosure,” one author says. Another wishes the Big Five “would get together and come up with a set of principles around AI that they intend to adhere to.” But some bestselling authors say their publishers’ use of AI is forcing them to consider publishing future books on their own.

“What are authors even doing with traditional publishers anymore if they’re going to outsource everything to a machine?” one bestselling author says. “Why can't an author do that themselves?”

items.title_zh: 麦克米伦为AI助手大办入职派对却迅速砍掉项目
items.summary_zh: 知名出版商麦克米伦曾为企业AI助手大搞欢迎派对并嘲讽人类员工，因频繁幻觉且体验糟糕，该项目不久后即遭弃用关停
items.article_content_zh:
2024年1月，麦克米伦出版公司位于下曼哈顿的总部上演了颇具讽刺意味的一幕。员工踏入办公大楼时，发现墙上贴满了欢迎“新团队成员”的宣传单，员工餐厅里更是布置了紫色气球、灯牌以及用甜甜圈拼成的标语，共同庆祝名为“NOA”的AI助手正式上线。然而，NOA的全称是“绝非普通助理（No Ordinary Assistant）”，这种充满挑衅意味的命名让公司内的多名真正的人类助理深感冒犯与不安。

根据管理层发送给员工的内部邮件，NOA是由德国软件公司Chaptr开发的企业级聊天机器人，而该软件公司正由麦克米伦的母公司霍尔茨布林克出版集团（Holtzbrinck）注资支持。管理层向员工保证，NOA是一个封闭安全的闭环环境，员工可以放心地将敏感商业资料输入其中，无需担心数据外泄或被用于模型二次训练。然而在随后举行的内部培训中，员工却被明确告知该AI频繁产生幻觉，给出的答案并不靠谱，必须时刻由人工进行事实核验。

原本被寄予厚望、旨在替代繁琐日常工作的AI工具，最终沦为员工不得不投入额外精力防范纠错的累赘。伴随着一线人员的强烈抵触和极低的实用转化率，这一场高调宣传的“企业AI革命”最终沦为昙花一现的公关自嗨，该系统在上线后不久便被公司彻底叫停关停。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 麦克米伦出版公司在其纽约总部为内部AI助手“NOA”大操大办入职欢迎派对，不仅在员工餐厅挂满气球横幅，还用甜甜圈拼出欢迎口号，其全称“绝非普通助理”引发人类助理的强烈反感。管理层极力推销这款由母公司投资的德国初创团队开发的企业聊天机器人，但员工在培训中被明确告知该AI漏洞百出且极易产生幻觉，必须依赖人工全程核查纠错。这场违背一线意愿的自嗨式AI实验迅速翻车，该工具上线后不久便因缺乏实用价值被悄然终止。

items.title: S-1: Anthropic had $112.4B in cash and $19.3B in short-term investments on June 30, surpassing every non-bank US company except Berkshire Hathaway and Alphabet (Leslie Picker/CNBC)
items.title_en: S-1: Anthropic had $112.4B in cash and $19.3B in short-term investments on June 30, surpassing every non-bank US company except Berkshire Hathaway and Alphabet (Leslie Picker/CNBC)
items.author: CNBC
items.article_content:
Anthropic has more cash than almost every company in America.

The nearly 6-year-old artificial intelligence lab disclosed on Monday in an S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission that it had $112.4 billion in cash, plus another $19.3 billion in short-term investments, as of June 30.

Anthropic's total of $131.7 billion surpasses every non-bank U.S. company, except for Berkshire Hathaway and Alphabet, according to data compiled by CNBC and S&P Capital IQ.

As of midyear, Anthropic had more cash than Amazon, SpaceX, Meta and Microsoft. It had more than Nvidia and Apple combined.

Depending on how much the company raises in its initial public offering — and reports suggest it could top $100 billion — Anthropic could bump its hoard to more than $230 billion in cash.

So far, Anthropic hasn't shared specific details about its offering size, and it said in the filing that existing investors would also be selling into the IPO – meaning the company itself won't collect the entire fundraise. Those details are expected to be disclosed in about two weeks.

Never before has a company gone public with anywhere near this amount of cash.

Anthropic's trove underscores the fundraising prowess that has allowed it to amass an aggregate of $141 billion in private financing in just six years since its founding. However, given the company's future commitments for computing power that have yet to hit its expenses, Anthropic will have to continue accumulating cash through fundraising or generating profits to fulfill its obligations.

Anthropic's first-half compute and infrastructure expenses totaled $8.95 billion. But the company said it usually buys computing power 12 to 18 months ahead of time, and only recognizes expenses as that capacity becomes available. That means the first-half expense figure doesn't capture the full scale of its future obligations.

As of June 30, Anthropic disclosed $321.4 billion in estimated future undiscounted lease obligations and $265.6 billion in expected future fixed or minimum-guaranteed commitments — more than half a trillion total. These will commence within the next few years, with terms ranging from one year to 20 years.

Additionally, the company said that subsequent to June 30, it entered into new and amended agreements with a minimum future payment obligation of about $245 billion.

The company hasn't shared an aggregate amount of its up-to-date commitments yet.

If Anthropic's cash is king, compute is its biggest claim on the crown.

—CNBC's Ritika Shah and Nick Wells contributed to this article.

items.article_content_zh:
Anthropic 拥有的现金比几乎所有美国公司都多。

这家成立近 6 年的人工智能实验室周一在向美国证券交易委员会提交的 S-1 文件中披露，截至 6 月 30 日，该实验室拥有 1124 亿美元现金，另外还有 193 亿美元的短期投资。

根据 CNBC 和 S&P Capital IQ 汇编的数据，Anthropic 的总资产为 1317 亿美元，超过了除伯克希尔哈撒韦公司和 Alphabet 之外的所有美国非银行公司。

截至年中，Anthropic 的现金超过了亚马逊、SpaceX、Meta 和微软。它的数量比英伟达和苹果的总和还要多。

根据公司在首次公开募股中筹集的金额（有报道称其可能超过 1000 亿美元），Anthropic 可能会将其现金储备增加到超过 2300 亿美元。

到目前为止，Anthropic 尚未透露有关其发行规模的具体细节，并且在文件中表示，现有投资者也将参与 IPO，这意味着该公司本身不会筹集全部资金。这些细节预计将在大约两周内披露。

此前从未有一家公司以如此数额的现金上市。

Anthropic 的财富凸显了其筹款能力，使其在成立短短六年内就筹集了总计 1,410 亿美元的私人融资。然而，鉴于该公司未来对计算能力的承诺尚未达到其支出，Anthropic 将不得不继续通过融资或产生利润来积累现金以履行其义务。

Anthropic 上半年的计算和基础设施支出总计 89.5 亿美元。但该公司表示，它通常会提前 12 到 18 个月购买计算能力，并且只有在该能力可用时才确认费用。这意味着上半年的支出数据并未反映其未来债务的全部规模。

截至 6 月 30 日，Anthropic 披露的预计未来未贴现租赁义务为 3,214 亿美元，预计未来固定或最低担保承诺为 2,656 亿美元，总计超过 5000 亿美元。这些将在未来几年内开始，期限从一年到二十年不等。

此外，该公司表示，6 月 30 日之后，它签订了新的和修订的协议，未来的最低付款义务约为 2,450 亿美元。

该公司尚未分享其最新承诺的总额。

如果说 Anthropic 的现金为王，那么计算能力就是其最大的优势。

—CNBC 的 Ritika Shah 和 Nick Wells 对本文做出了贡献。

items.title: AI Emergency Alerts Are Coming. Humans Might Not Be Ready
items.title_en: AI Emergency Alerts Are Coming. Humans Might Not Be Ready
items.author: Wired AI
items.article_content:
This story was produced by Grist and copublished with WIRED. It is part of Distorted, a Grist series exploring the spread of misinformation in the wake of extreme weather, and is published with support from the CO2 Foundation.

Earlier this month, after Hurricane Isaias made landfall on the Gulf Coast as a Category 3 hurricane, the emergency management expert Laura Myers got a call from a meteorologist in Alabama. Myers is director of the University of Alabama’s Center for Advanced Public Safety, and she talks to state and local emergency managers around her region all the time. The meteorologist told Myers that a local emergency manager had published a graphic showing where Isaias might threaten the Alabama coast with a “sting jet” of high winds.

The problem? The emergency manager had generated the graphic using an artificial intelligence chatbot, and it wasn’t accurate.

“That county emergency manager was trying to get his stakeholders to focus on the risk in that county, and so he had asked AI to help him,” she said. “It did what he wanted it to do, but it was not meteorologically accurate.”

Most emergency management agencies don’t permit employees to use generative AI, but Myers and most other emergency management experts agree that its usage is likely already pervasive at state and local disaster departments. There are hundreds of companies that are marketing AI tools to emergency managers for tasks like flood damage assessment and resource coordination, but public communication is one of the areas where government employees and startups have the most interest.

Emergency department personnel with the city of New York monitor the watch-command room in Brooklyn on February 23, 2026, ahead of a winter storm.

The reason? Most emergency managers aren’t very good at sending out alerts and quickly communicating about disasters with the public. That’s not because they’re emergency managers, but because they are human beings. They tend to write in jargon that non-experts might not understand, leave out information on the assumption that the public already knows it, and include irrelevant details that could distract people from what they actually do need to know.

“A lot of agencies are really limited in resources and the number of people that they have,” said Jeannette Sutton, a disaster researcher at the University of Albany who has created a comprehensive dashboard that provides templates for disaster alerts. “I think they recognize it as a priority, but they don't prioritize it until they realize they should have. They're just trying to get their job done without screwing something up.”

Emergency managers are the government officials who are in charge of disaster response and recovery. At the state and local level, It is these officials and their agencies, not the Federal Emergency Management Agency, that make up the first line of defense after an extreme weather event. As such, emergency managers often like to say that “trust is our currency,” and it’s in their communication with the public that they build and lose this trust.

As climate disasters become more frequent and widespread, there have been numerous examples of flawed human communication scrambling an emergency response. In 2016, for instance, adjacent counties in California issued a “voluntary evacuation” and a “mandatory evacuation” for the same wildfire. In Australia in 2019, officials warned about wildfires by using the phrase “Watch and Act,” which the government later said caused “significant confusion” because no one knew what it meant.

In some cases, inadequate communication can mean the difference between life and death. This happened in Montecito, California, after the 2017 Thomas Fire. A few weeks after the fire, a heavy rainstorm produced a deadly mudslide. The government of Santa Barbara County struggled to communicate the risk to residents still traumatized from the blaze and experiencing a phenomenon that Sutton calls “warning fatigue.” The county sent alerts to everyone in the “voluntary evacuation zone” for wildfires, telling residents to “stay alert to changing conditions and be prepared to leave immediately.” Most of those residents should have left immediately, but to many the evacuation notice was optional; others just didn’t want to evacuate for a second time in a month. The mudslide killed 23 people and injured more than 160 others.

Governments that put out bad warnings are apt to lose the public’s trust, said Sutton. “They're losing the opportunity to be that voice to help people to be safe.”

In theory, alerts are a perfect use case for artificial intelligence, and in particular for the generative AI systems that have developed at a dramatic pace over the past few years. FEMA provides training sessions for emergency managers to learn best practices for synthesizing and sending alerts, but many officials don’t remember all their training when an emergency arrives. A large language model is different. It can read hundreds of thousands of alerts in mere minutes, digest all the research on what works in similar scenarios, and then apply that to edit a human alert in seconds.

“If you’ve only sent one [alert] in your life, and that was 15 years ago, and you need to remember all your training, and you’re thinking ‘Hey, there's a chemical plume coming my way, the phone's ringing, the radio's blaring, I need help,’ the AI is probably gonna do a better job than you are,” said Rob Dale, a former meteorologist who now runs the emergency management department in Ingham County, Michigan.

Dale has already used AI to draft a few practice alerts behind the scenes, but he’s never had to send one out. Ingham County is a small county in central Michigan, and it’s immune from major weather events like hurricanes and fires. If such an event did happen, Dale said he would have no issue allowing a chatbot to draft his incident communication, but he’d still want control over sending the alert out.

Some experts believe the technology is already good enough to deploy. EM1, a startup that produces AI software for emergency managers, has used Sutton’s research to train a model that its executives say is already better than almost any human emergency manager. The company has tested this in-house model on a number of scenarios including wildfires and tsunamis. It can already match or exceed human capabilities on most benchmark tests.

Sutton gave Grist an example of how the software works: Grist provided her with a recent alert sent by a New Mexico county that was trying to warn residents about flooding on the San Juan River.

After a series of erroneous evacuation alerts to L.A. residents sparked panic during an active wildfire season in January 2025, the director of the county’s emergency management department apologized.

The original alert read, “Breeched banks. The water is rising. EVACUATE NOW. McGee Park open for people and pets, RV.” Sutton asked the EM1 model to evaluate and revise the alert. In a few seconds, it produced what she said is a far better alert, one that checks all the main boxes of disaster communication.

The new alert read: “San Juan County: Floodwater is rising near [location]. People in [evacuation area]: LEAVE NOW for higher ground. Do not walk or drive through floodwater. McGee Park is open for people and pets. Check [official update source] for updates.” The model identified and fixed several problems with the original text, which does not say who is sending the alert, name the specific location where flooding is happening, or clarify who needs to evacuate and give advice on how to do so safely. It misspells the word “breached,” and it doesn’t provide any guidance on where residents can seek further information.

EM1 has contracts with around a hundred government agencies and school districts, but none are using it to automate their extreme weather alerts just yet. For the moment, they’re only using it to workshop plans and internal preparations. Even so, all the experts interviewed for this story said they are certain that many emergency managers are already using chatbots to write messages, even if they won’t admit it. Sutton said that the emergency managers who take her alert training sessions often present her with high-quality alerts they have drafted in seconds using ChatGPT or Gemini.

“Official adoption is pretty low, but people are unofficially using it, absolutely,” said Sarah Miller, a professor of emergency management at Pierce College in Florida and a longtime instructor at the National Disaster Preparedness Training Center. “They're using their own personal accounts, or they're using free ones.”

It sounds like an easy trade-off: if AI is better and faster than humans, and the difference between a good alert and a bad alert can be life and death, we should be using AI for every heat wave and wildfire. Yet even researchers who are bullish on chatbot technology say that making the switch could backfire. Members of the public who are skeptical of AI or who don’t trust the government in the first place may spurn agencies that publish AI-generated graphics or social media posts. In Syracuse, New York, for instance, a union of public employees sued the local government for using an AI service to answer non-emergency 911 calls.

As is the case in other areas where AI is being deployed, disaster experts say that for the moment the software is only as capable as the person using it. A seasoned emergency manager might be able to speed up their communication with the public by having a chatbot draft a series of alerts, but an inexperienced one rushing to create an urgent alert won’t know how to evaluate the output of a model like ChatGPT or Claude.

Even though the technology is a ways off from being able to perform without a human expert in the loop, that hasn’t stopped many understaffed emergency management departments from using it. As for how the proliferation of AI-generated content is affecting public trust in government, experts say it’s too early to tell.

“If you had a human sending you a text message versus a computer sending you a text message, which one would you believe is being more accurate?” said Justin Snair, the founder of Preppr, another company that offers AI software to emergency managers.

The answer, he said, depends on the person receiving it.

Earlier this month, after Hurricane Isaias made landfall on the Gulf Coast as a Category 3 hurricane, the emergency management expert Laura Myers got a call from a meteorologist in Alabama. Myers is director of the University of Alabama’s Center for Advanced Public Safety
items.summary_en: During a recent hurricane landfall on the US Gulf Coast, a local emergency manager bypassed agency rules to generate a disaster hazard map using an AI chatbot, aiming to heighten local risk awareness. However, the resulting graphic fabricated high-wind danger zones that were completely inaccurate meteorologically. While emergency agencies officially prohibit generative AI, frontline staff cutting corners highlights severe public safety vulnerabilities caused by unverified AI hallucinations.

items.article_content_zh:
基层应急专家透露，在飓风过境期间，有地方防灾负责人为了让辖区利益相关方迅速感知危险，私下指使AI生成了一张显示致命阵风的警报图。AI如实满足了其‘看起来很危险’的指令需求，但在气象科学层面毫无依据。

专家警告，当公众生命财产依赖官方预警信号时，把关机制缺失的‘AI造图’将直接瓦解官方公信力，甚至引发致命的误导性恐慌或不当撤离。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 在飓风侵袭美国沿海期间，一名基层应急管理官员擅自利用AI聊天机器人生成灾害预警图并公开发布，试图以此引起当地民众和决策层对本区域灾情的重视。然而，该AI图表呈现的高风速危险区在气象学上纯属凭空捏造。尽管绝大多数应急机构明令禁止使用未经验证的生成式AI工具，但前线人员为了图省事走捷径，正让虚假预警对公共安全造成难以挽回的二次伤害。

items.title: SK Hynix expects memory shortages to persist through at least 2030; it has long-term deals with 14 major buyers for 50%+ of its output in 2027 and 2028 (Simon Sharwood/The Register)
items.title_en: SK Hynix expects memory shortages to persist through at least 2030; it has long-term deals with 14 major buyers for 50%+ of its output in 2027 and 2028 (Simon Sharwood/The Register)
items.author: The Register
items.article_content:
Simon Sharwood Simon Sharwood APAC Editor Published wed 28 Oct 2026 // 04:21 UTC Make us preferred on Google READ MORE AI slows growth for Infosys and keeps it afloat at the same time 2 hours ago Big Red gets cozy with Google to offer TPUs to AI customers 8 hours ago Anthropic now lets Claude users jump out of plane without parachute 8 hours ago AI 'hacker' finds 4 severe bugs in popular industrial control software in under 4 hours 9 hours ago A whopping 3% of boardroom execs spy productivity and costs savings from AI 14 hours ago Korean memory-maker SK Hynix has predicted memory shortages will persist until at least the year 2030 and says that will help it to boost its already exceptional revenue and profits to new levels.

In remarks published on Wednesday alongside its quarterly results, the company offered its belief that “a virtuous cycle has taken hold in which AI-driven productivity gains and new revenue generation in areas such as software development, customer service, and search lead to greater AI adoption, which in turn drives increased investment in infrastructure.”

SK Hynix thinks this is great news, because it means more buyers are entering the market for AI infrastructure, including “general enterprises” and nations building sovereign infrastructure. In coming years, the company sees even more demand for memory coming from autonomous cars and the growing robotics market.

While the company is working hard to build more factories and get them working, execs admitted it can’t do that fast enough to meet demand.

“The company assessed that supply … is not keeping pace with the growth of the market,” SK Hynix told investors. “Given technical difficulty of leading-edge processes and the long lead time required to build new production facilities, it expects the structure in which demand exceeds supply to persist through 2030.”

It gets worse. SK Hynix has 14 long-term deals with 14 big buyers, who will collectively buy more than half of its output during 2027 and 2028, and some of them want to extend those agreements. The Korean giant doesn’t mind that because the deals include “a mechanism that reflects market conditions within a price range agreed upon with customers” and give it “a structure that secures stable profitability while allowing flexible responses to market changes.”

Those deals helped SK Hynix to record quarterly revenue of ₩104.6 trillion ($78.1 billion), up 328 percent year-over-year and 32 percent quarter-over-quarter. Operating profit came in at ₩87.68 trillion ($62.8 billion), up 486 percent year over year.

The company told investors it’s not done yet, outlining plans to expand production and emphasize lucrative products that will “scale up revenue and profit one step further next year.”

Doing so will likely dent profits elsewhere, because on the company’s earnings call, chief financial officer Kim Woo-hyun predicted “shipment volumes for PCs and mobile devices are expected to decrease due to cost burdens from rising memory prices and supply shortages.”

Increasing HBM4 production, which it believes will “surpass HBM3E in both shipment volume and revenue in the fourth quarter and … establish itself as a mainstream product.”

“Rapidly” increasing the portion of its 10nm-class 6th generation (1c) process technology and expand sales of DDR5 and LPDDR5 SOCAMM for AI servers.

Developing NAND “into a core solution that enhances the throughput and economic efficiency of AI services, based on HBF and system optimization technologies.”

Investors liked what they heard, with some apparently seeing the memory-maker’s outlook as suggesting the AI boom won’t sputter out any time soon and sent the company’s share price up by about three percent in after-hours trading. ®

items.article_content_zh:
Simon Sharwood Simon Sharwood 亚太区编辑 发布时间 2026 年 10 月 28 日// 04:21 UTC 让我们在 Google 上成为首选 阅读更多 人工智能减缓了 Infosys 的增长，同时保持其运转 2 小时前 Big Red 与 Google 合作，向 AI 客户提供 TPU 8 小时前 Anthropic 现在允许 Claude 用户在不使用降落伞的情况下跳出飞机 8 小时前 AI“黑客”发现了 4 个严重错误不到 4 小时 9 小时前 多达 3% 的董事会高管在 14 小时前发现人工智能带来的生产力和成本节省 韩国内存制造商 SK 海力士预测内存短缺将持续到至少 2030 年，并表示这将有助于将其本已出色的收入和利润提高到新的水平。

在周三发布的季度业绩报告中，该公司表示相信“良性循环已经形成，人工智能驱动的生产力提高和软件开发、客户服务和搜索等领域的新收入创造导致了人工智能的更广泛采用，进而推动了基础设施投资的增加。”

SK海力士认为这是个好消息，因为这意味着更多买家正在进入人工智能基础设施市场，包括“一般企业”和建设主权基础设施的国家。未来几年，该公司预计自动驾驶汽车和不断增长的机器人市场对内存的需求将会更大。

尽管该公司正在努力建设更多工厂并让其投入运营，但高管们承认，它的速度还不够快，无法满足需求。

SK 海力士告诉投资者：“公司评估供应……跟不上市场增长的步伐。” “鉴于领先工艺的技术难度以及建设新生产设施所需的较长交货时间，预计需求超过供应的结构将持续到 2030 年。”

情况变得更糟。 SK 海力士与 14 个大买家签订了 14 项长期协议，这些买家将在 2027 年和 2028 年期间总共购买其一半以上的产量，其中一些买家希望延长这些协议。这家韩国巨头并不介意，因为这些交易包括“一种在与客户商定的价格范围内反映市场状况的机制”，并赋予其“一种确保稳定盈利能力同时灵活应对市场变化的结构”。

这些交易帮助 SK 海力士创下了 104.6 万亿韩元（781 亿美元）的季度收入记录，同比增长 328%，环比增长 32%。营业利润达 87.68 万亿韩元（628 亿美元），同比增长 486%。

该公司告诉投资者，尚未完成，概述了扩大生产的计划，并强调利润丰厚的产品，这些产品将“在明年进一步扩大收入和利润”。

这样做可能会削弱其他地方的利润，因为在该公司的财报电话会议上，首席财务官 Kim Woo-hyun 预测“由于内存价格上涨和供应短缺带来的成本负担，个人电脑和移动设备的出货量预计将减少。”

增加 HBM4 产量，它相信“第四季度的出货量和收入将超过 HBM3E，并……确立其作为主流产品的地位。”

“迅速”增加其10纳米级第六代（1c）工艺技术的份额，并扩大用于AI服务器的DDR5和LPDDR5 SOCAMM的销售。

将 NAND 开发为“基于 HBF 和系统优化技术，提高人工智能服务吞吐量和经济效率的核心解决方案”。

投资者喜欢他们所听到的，一些人显然认为这家存储器制造商的前景表明人工智能热潮不会很快消失，并导致该公司股价在盘后交易中上涨约 3%。 ®

items.title: Should AI Decide Your Court Case? This Judge Says Yes
items.title_en: Should AI Decide Your Court Case? This Judge Says Yes
items.author: Wired AI
items.article_content:
In a few days, judge Geoffrey Vos will retire as Master of the Rolls, the most senior position in England’s civil justice system. As one of his final acts, he’s trying to stoke a debate about whether—and how—judges should be using artificial intelligence.

Under the latest guidance, judges in England are advised to confine their use of AI to administrative tasks, and Vos tells WIRED he uses Microsoft Copilot all the time to locate far-flung documents and summarize large bodies of text. But recently, he visited a court in Shenzhen, China, where civil disputes are already being decided by judges with heavy assistance from AI. Impressed by what he saw, Vos believes that courts across the globe should consider following.

That road is littered with pitfalls. Multiple lawyers have been caught citing case law hallucinated by AI, and in a first for the UK, somebody recently lost their license to practice in part because they misused the technology. Meanwhile, with chatbots as their legal counsel, litigants are flooding the courts with an unprecedented number of claims, some of them bogus.

Yet Vos remains convinced that AI will someday help resolve civil disputes more rapidly and in ways that cost far less. While complicated commercial disputes and sensitive family cases might require a human judge, he believes that personal injury claims, low-value professional negligence cases, and the like could easily be adjudicated by AI.

“What most people desperately want in civil disputes is resolution,” Vos tells WIRED. “The question is, where is the line to be drawn?”

Given his impending retirement, the debate for Vos is largely a philosophical one. But for everyone else in the profession—and for coders, cybersecurity experts, math professors, and a whole host of others—the rules are changing fast.

In October, WIRED met with Vos at his office at the Royal Courts of Justice, London. We discussed the ways that AI is spilling into the courts, the practical and ethical issues it raises, and how the justice system might adapt to serve a new generation raised alongside the technology.

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

WIRED: You’re just a few days away from retirement. How do you feel about leaving the post at this particular juncture, as AI begins to reshape how law is practiced and justice administered?

GEOFFREY VOS: When I started as a lawyer, we had foolscap paper, typists, and Tipp-Ex. We moved rapidly into word processors, faxes, and eventually computers.

Lawyers are conservative with a lowercase c. But that doesn’t mean that they should be backward-looking or retrogressive. It means they should be adopting change cautiously, with their eyes open.

The legal system is for the people of this country. You can’t be effective in providing access to justice if you’re not on the same technological wavelength. But it’s time to leave it to a new generation of leadership judges.

I don’t use it for writing judgments, but I use it for finding things out, navigating large quantities of material, and checking things. It saves me time. I have 11 meetings a day. I know there’s a document created years ago that’s relevant to my meeting—and Copilot finds it in seconds. I do that every day.

In law, isn’t the devil always in the details? Doesn’t confidence in the legal system depend on the understanding that a judge will review and consider every inch of every court submission?

People have confidence in our justice system because they believe that our judges have absolute integrity. In order not to lose that integrity, you have to explain how you’re adopting technology and achieve a broad consensus that it is appropriate.

How is AI spilling into the courts right now? Is it changing how litigants and legal professionals behave? What issues is it throwing up?

It’s changing everything remarkably quickly. We see a 10 percent rise in the number of county court cases started every year—and it looks as if this may increase. That’s because everybody who has a legal problem now puts it into Gemini, ChatGPT, or Claude. Ask it to create a particulars of claim, a case, a claim form—it can.

What proportion of these claims are based on sound legal principles, though? How often are people led by a chatbot to mistakenly believe they have a claim?

We don’t have the data. But I think it’s a mistake to assume that just because a claim is created by AI, it’s totally frivolous.

In a way it’s a good problem, because it shows there’s greater access to justice because of technology. One of the problems with justice in the past is that it’s only been available to rich people.

If people have a problem sufficient to bother ChatGPT, they probably genuinely think they have a claim. When you explore their problem in detail, you might find it is actually a bit different, but it may still be a legal problem and may still be reasonable for them to have wanted to bring it to attention.

People are not generally time wasters. They’re not generally trying to make trouble.

What about the opportunity for AI to fabricate evidence on which judges have previously been able to rely—images, video, voice recordings? Where does that leave the courts?

Often, judges have to decide whether a person is telling the truth. That is the most difficult thing to do, because humans are not bad at lying. But judges make these decisions every day. There’s absolutely no difference—in scale or qualitatively—in somebody producing a false image created by AI.

The only reason we’re all getting so excited about deepfakes is because they are so new. But actually, that is the stuff of judging.

But we’re talking about a whole category of evidence that’s now somewhat compromised. Doesn’t that affect a judge’s ability to decide whether somebody is lying?

It was always thus. We always had to decide whether wills were forged, because people used to do that. It’s exactly the same with voice recordings, and video. It’s just an extension of the type of false information that is produced to the court.

People will find out when they produce fake images to the court that they are committing perjury and they will go to prison, just as if they’d forged a will.

I think we need to be cautious about predicting disaster. I’m very optimistic.

You’ve previously described an “inevitable” future where simpler civil cases are adjudicated entirely by AI. Why are you confident that’s where we’re headed?

You need to find a way to deliver justice that is within the cultural grain. That doesn’t mean you just conduct all your cases on TikTok. But if you don’t understand that people are asking LLMs for the answer to almost every question under the sun, including legal questions, you’re likely to get it wrong when you try to devise a process fit for the 21st century.

It’s all about consensus. It will only be possible to ask people to accept algorithmic decision-making if they consent to the process in a particular case, or if society decides through legislation.

When people go to court and get an adverse outcome, even if they regard the outcome as idiosyncratic or even wrong, when it’s delivered in a human way, it can be accepted over time. With AI, we have to be careful; it may be less easy for people to accept an adverse machine-driven decision.

I very much want to see a very open, international discussion about how we should resolve disputes.

I suspect part of the reason people object to trial by AI is because we can’t know precisely how a model has arrived at a decision. What’s to be done about this problem of explainability?
items.original_content:
In a few days, judge Geoffrey Vos will retire as Master of the Rolls, the most senior position in England’s civil justice system. As one of his final acts, he’s trying to stoke a debate about whether—and how—judges should be using artificial intelligence.

Under the latest guidance, judges in England are advised to confine their use of AI to administrative tasks, and Vos tells WIRED he uses Microsoft Copilot all the time to locate far-flung documents and summarize large bodies of text. But recently, he visited a court in Shenzhen, China, where civil disputes are already being decided by judges with heavy assistance from AI. Impressed by what he saw, Vos believes that courts across the globe should consider following.

That road is littered with pitfalls. Multiple lawyers have been caught citing case law hallucinated by AI, and in a first for the UK, somebody recently lost their license to practice in part because they misused the technology. Meanwhile, with chatbots as their legal counsel, litigants are flooding the courts with an unprecedented number of claims, some of them bogus.

items.title_zh: 英国资深大法官临退发声：力挺法庭用AI辅助判案
items.summary_zh: 英格兰民事司法最高主管即将退休之际呼吁全球法院拥抱AI审判，称深圳法庭的高效经验值得借鉴
items.article_content_zh:
英格兰民事司法体系的最高掌门人、民事上诉法院院长杰弗里·沃斯即将在数日后正式退休。作为其职业生涯的收尾举动，他选择打破保守惯例，公开掀起一场关于法官是否以及如何运用人工智能协助审判的全球大讨论。目前英国官方的最新指引仍将AI严格限定在排期、检索等行政性任务中，沃斯本人也坦承自己每天依赖微软Copilot在海量文书中进行跨库检索与内容提炼。

促使这位老牌法官观念发生质变的，是他近期对中国深圳法院的实地考察。在深圳，大量复杂民事争议已经在AI算法的高强度辅助下由法官快速完成定分止争。亲眼目睹这套高自动化系统的高效运转后，沃斯明确表态，认为全球司法系统都应当摆脱偏见并跟进这一趋势，将AI从打杂助手升级为实质性的裁判工具。

然而，司法全面拥抱技术的前路荆棘密布。近期英美多起法庭诉讼中，多名出庭律师因直接搬用聊天机器人胡编乱造的虚构案例而惨遭重罚，英国甚至刚刚出现了首位因滥用AI生成假法条而被直接吊销执业资格的律师。与此同时，大量缺乏专业背景的当事人将通用大模型作为廉价法律代理人，炮制出史无前例的垃圾诉状洪流挤爆法庭立案系统。即便如此，沃斯依旧坚称，AI带来的阵痛无法掩盖其极速化解民事积案的巨大潜力。

items.title: Sources: CXMT plans to start HBM3E production despite yields of just 20% to 30%; its HBM3E performance is closer to that of SK Hynix's previous-gen HBM3 chips (Reuters)
items.title_en: Sources: CXMT plans to start HBM3E production despite yields of just 20% to 30%; its HBM3E performance is closer to that of SK Hynix's previous-gen HBM3 chips (Reuters)
items.author: Reuters
items.original_content:
Reuters:
Sources: CXMT plans to start HBM3E production despite yields of just 20% to 30%; its HBM3E performance is closer to that of SK Hynix's previous-gen HBM3 chips  —  China's CXMT plans to start production of HBM3E, an advanced type of high-bandwidth memory c
items.content_snippet: China's CXMT plans to start production of HBM3E, an advanced type of high-bandwidth memory chip used with AI processors …
items.summary_en: Chinese memory giant CXMT is preparing to initiate production of advanced HBM3E chips to supply domestic AI accelerators facing severe supply bottlenecks. The move comes despite current manufacturing yields lingering between just 20% and 30%, with actual performance closer to SK Hynix's previous-generation HBM3. Facing stringent export controls, the foundry is willing to absorb high scrap rates to establish a sovereign silicon foothold.
items.title_zh: 长鑫存储传量产高带宽内存：良率不足三成且性能对标旧代
items.summary_zh: 长鑫存储拟启动高带宽内存量产，尽管良率仅两至三成且性能接近竞品前代，仍强行填补本土算力短缺

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 国内存储芯片龙头长鑫存储正推进先进高带宽内存HBM3E的量产计划，力求缓解本土人工智能芯片对关键存储组件的极度渴求。相关产业动态显示其当前制造良率仅在20%至30%之间，且实际综合性能更接近SK海力士上一代HBM3水准。在外部先进制程封锁与供应链严密防线之下，企业选择承担高昂报废成本强行开跑，以抢占本土替代的战略生态位。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Chinese memory giant CXMT is preparing to initiate production of advanced HBM3E chips to supply domestic AI accelerators facing severe supply bottlenecks. The move comes despite current manufacturing yields lingering between just 20% and 30%, with actual performance closer to SK Hynix's previous-generation HBM3. Facing stringent export controls, the foundry is willing to absorb high scrap rates to establish a sovereign silicon foothold.

elements_zh.what: 拟顶着20%-30%的超低良率强推HBM3E量产，产品实际性能接近行业龙头上一代HBM3
elements_zh.why: 海外先进制程封锁严峻，国内AI芯片极度缺芯，急需不计代价打破垄断实现自主供给

elements_en.where: Domestic semiconductor fabrication and advanced packaging lines in China
elements_en.what: Plans to produce HBM3E memory chips despite low yields of 20%-30% and performance resembling prior-gen HBM3
elements_en.why: Severe export curbs on high-end chips require accelerating domestic self-sufficiency for AI accelerators at all costs

ai_analysis.insight_zh: “只要良率不为零，那就叫自主突破；只要芯片能点亮，名字就敢跟顶流平齐。”在卡脖子的窒息感面前，两三成的良率已经不算工业瑕疵，而是沉甸甸的战略买路钱——毕竟先解决“有没有”，再去挑剔“好不好”，历来是科技突围战里最悲壮也最真实的剧本。
ai_analysis.insight_en: In the shadow of harsh tech embargoes, a 20% yield isn't an engineering failure—it's the steep admission fee for technological sovereignty. Leaping straight to an HBM3E label while delivering HBM3 performance proves that having a subpar chip to boot up beats having zero chips on the rack every single day.

items.title: Jio Platforms, India's largest telecom and digital services company, rose 21.4% in its trading debut after raising ~$3.2B in the country's largest IPO (Priyanka Salve/CNBC)
items.title_en: Jio Platforms, India's largest telecom and digital services company, rose 21.4% in its trading debut after raising ~$3.2B in the country's largest IPO (Priyanka Salve/CNBC)
items.author: CNBC
items.article_content:
India's largest telecom and digital services player had offered 270 million shares in the IPO priced at 1,119 rupees apiece, raising 302 billion rupees ($3.2 billion) in the country's largest-ever IPO.

Global brokerage Nomura on Wednesday gave Jio Platforms a buy rating, setting a target price of 1,340 rupees, implying an upside of 19.7% to its IPO price. The brokerage said in a report that Jio's capex cycle is largely over and there is expected to be a sharp improvement in the company's free cash flow.

Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's flagship company, Reliance Industries, owns more than a 66% stake in Jio Platforms, followed by Meta Platforms' affiliate Jaadhu Holdings that owns nearly 10% and Google International, which owns 7.7%, as per LSEG data.

items.title_zh: 印度电信巨头吉奥平台上市首日暴涨逾21%
items.summary_zh: 印度电信巨头吉奥平台完成当地史上最大规模32亿美元募资，挂牌交易首日股价大涨21.4%
items.article_content_zh:
作为印度首富穆克什·安巴尼旗下信实工业的核心数字业务板块，吉奥平台在此次公开招股中以每股1119卢比的价格发售了2.7亿股股票，总募集金额达到3020亿卢比（约合32亿美元），正式打破印度资本市场有史以来的首次公开募股募资规模纪录。

上市首日，华尔街投行野村证券便直接给予吉奥平台买入评级，并将目标价定为1340卢比，预示着较发行价仍有近20%的上涨空间。券商研报特别指出，吉奥在5G与光纤网络铺设等方面的巨额资本支出周期已经大体收尾，随之而来的将是公司自由现金流的爆发式改善，这为其后续的盈利变现提供了坚实支撑。

股权结构方面，母公司信实工业依然保持着绝对控制权，持股比例超过66%。值得注意的是，硅谷两大科技巨头此前便已深度绑定该标的——Meta旗下投资实体持有近10%的股份，而谷歌国际则持有约7.7%，这为吉奥未来在数字生态、移动支付与人工智能应用的本土落地提供了强大的技术与生态底盘。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 印度最大电信及数字服务商吉奥平台完成该国历史上规模最大的首次公开募股，以每股1119卢比筹集约32亿美元，并在上市交易首日大涨21.4%。依托信实工业控股逾66%、以及脸书母公司Meta和谷歌合计近18%的战略持股，吉奥平台凭借基础设施建设高投资期的结束，展现出自由现金流大幅改善的强劲预期，引发二级市场资本疯抢。

Backed by Reliance Industries along with strategic stakes from Meta and Google, the company attracted massive market demand as its heavy capital expenditure cycle nears completion, paving the way for surging free cash flow.

items.title: Sources: Fujifilm plans to increase magnetic tape production capacity fivefold to meet AI-driven storage demand, its biggest production expansion in ~20 years (Nikkei Asia)
items.title_en: Sources: Fujifilm plans to increase magnetic tape production capacity fivefold to meet AI-driven storage demand, its biggest production expansion in ~20 years (Nikkei Asia)
items.author: Nikkei Asia
items.original_content: TOKYO -- Fujifilm will raise production capacity for magnetic tape fivefold to meet artificial-intelligence-driven demand, marking the company's largest investment to make the data storage medium in roughly 20 years, Nikkei has learned.
items.content_snippet: TOKYO -- Fujifilm will raise production capacity for magnetic tape fivefold to meet artificial-intelligence-driven demand, marking the company's largest investment to make the data storage medium in roughly 20 years, Nikkei has learned.
items.summary_en: To meet the explosive demand for long-term archiving driven by artificial intelligence, Fujifilm plans to quintuple its magnetic tape production capacity in its largest expansion for the storage medium in roughly 20 years. As AI training datasets and regulatory compliance require astronomical volumes of cold data to be preserved, tech hyperscalers are turning back to tape for its unmatched durability, zero-idle power consumption, and extreme cost efficiency.
items.title_zh: 富士胶片拟扩产磁带五倍应对AI海量存储需求
items.summary_zh: 富士胶片宣布近二十年来最大扩产计划，将磁带产能提高至五倍，以应对人工智能引发的海量冷数据归档需求

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 为应对全球人工智能浪潮带来的海量数据长期归档需求，富士胶片决定将其磁带产能大幅扩增至目前的五倍。这是该公司约20年来在磁带存储介质领域的最大单笔扩产动作。面对大模型训练和合规留存所催生的天文级冷数据，具备低功耗、长寿命及极高成本效益的磁带正在重新成为科技巨头与数据中心的战略级存储底盘。

Wall Street Journal:
Anthropic's S-1 implies a $40T+ annual TAM based the economic value of knowledge work in 2025, topping SpaceX's $28.5T estimate, without explicitly naming it  —  The company's estimated market opportunity, tied to the economic value of work pr
items.content_snippet: The company's estimated market opportunity, tied to the economic value of work produced by knowledge workers, tops SpaceX's enormous figure from earlier this year
items.summary_en: Anthropic's IPO registration document positions its total addressable market at over $40 trillion, based on the global economic value of knowledge work. This move aims to justify massive valuations by outscaling SpaceX's market projections, banking on AI's potential to replace human cognitive labor.

items.title: Sources: HP, Asus, and Acer are shifting some PC production from Thailand and Vietnam back to China amid rising component costs; Dell is mulling a similar move (Nikkei Asia)
items.title_en: Sources: HP, Asus, and Acer are shifting some PC production from Thailand and Vietnam back to China amid rising component costs; Dell is mulling a similar move (Nikkei Asia)
items.author: Nikkei Asia
items.article_content:
HP and Asus are among PC makers returning some production to China after building facilities in Vietnam and Thailand as part of a "China+1" diversification strategy. (Illustration by Michael Tsang)

TAIPEI -- Leading PC makers, including HP of the U.S. and Asus and Acer of Taiwan, are combating soaring component costs by shifting some production from Thailand and Vietnam back to China and using a new generation of contract manufacturers.
items.original_content:

TAIPEI -- Leading PC makers, including HP of the U.S. and Asus and Acer of Taiwan, are combating soaring component costs by shifting some production from Thailand and Vietnam back to China and using a new generation of contract manufacturers.
items.content_snippet:
HP and Asus are among PC makers returning some production to China after building facilities in Vietnam and Thailand as part of a "China+1" diversification strategy. (Illustration by Michael Tsang)

TAIPEI -- Leading PC makers, including HP of the U.S. and Asus and Acer of Taiwan, are combating soaring component costs by shifting some production from Thailand and Vietnam back to China and using a new generation of contract manufacturers.
items.summary_en: Facing soaring operational costs and supply chain inefficiencies in Southeast Asia, major PC manufacturers including HP, Asus, and Acer are shifting some production lines back to China. This pivot signals a retreat from 'China+1' strategies as financial realities override diversification goals.
items.title_zh: PC厂商供应链撤回中国，去全球化已成定局
items.summary_zh: 由于供应链成本高昂，惠普、华硕等PC大厂正将部分产能从东南亚迁回中国，放弃之前的避险策略

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 面对东南亚运营成本飙升及供应链效率低下的压力，惠普、华硕、宏碁等PC行业巨头正在进行战略调整，将部分生产线回迁至中国。这一动作标志着企业在经历数年的“中国+1”多元化布局后，因现实的财务压力不得不向全球制造效率最优解低头。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Facing soaring operational costs and supply chain inefficiencies in Southeast Asia, major PC manufacturers including HP, Asus, and Acer are shifting some production lines back to China. This pivot signals a retreat from 'China+1' strategies as financial realities override diversification goals.

elements_zh.where: 全球PC供应链布局
elements_zh.what: 将部分生产线从泰国和越南迁回中国
elements_zh.why: 因东南亚建厂运营成本激增，试图通过回迁恢复供应链的成本优势

elements_en.what: Moving parts of production back to China from Thailand and Vietnam
elements_en.why: Soaring operational costs in SE Asia are forcing a return to more cost-efficient manufacturing hubs

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 当初为了避险信誓旦旦去东南亚，现在因为降本增效又灰溜溜搬回来，资本的‘去风险’在‘真实的账单’面前显得如此苍白。这就是所谓的供应链全球化折腾了半天，最终发现中国还是那个无法逾越的生产力天花板。
ai_analysis.insight_en: After spending years pretending that moving to SE Asia was about 'strategic diversification,' these giants are now sheepishly crawling back because, surprise, the spreadsheets don't lie. It turns out that when the real bills are due, ideology loses to the sheer efficiency of Chinese manufacturing.

items.article_content_zh:
作为“中国+1”多元化战略的一部分，惠普和华硕等个人电脑制造商在越南和泰国建设工厂后将部分生产返回中国。 （曾俊华插画）

台北——包括美国惠普、台湾华硕和宏碁在内的领先个人电脑制造商正在通过将部分生产从泰国和越南转移回中国以及使用新一代合同制造商来应对零部件成本飙升的问题。

【起因与机理】因东南亚建厂运营成本激增，试图通过回迁恢复供应链的成本优势

【观点态度】这就是所谓的供应链全球化折腾了半天，最终发现中国还是那个无法逾越的生产力天花板。

items.content_snippet: The Federal Communications Commission said on Tuesday it approved Amazon (AMZN.O) Leo's $11.5 billion deal to acquire Globalstar (GSAT.O) …

items.title: Letter: two Democratic senators allege the Trump administration withheld a secret FISC ruling on search filters that let analysts access Americans' messages (Dell Cameron/Wired)
items.title_en: Letter: two Democratic senators allege the Trump administration withheld a secret FISC ruling on search filters that let analysts access Americans' messages (Dell Cameron/Wired)
items.author: Wired
items.article_content:
Two Democratic senators who have long overseen US intelligence say the Trump administration is illegally withholding a secret court’s findings from Congress until lawmakers renew a program that lets federal agents read Americans’ communications without a warrant.

Seven months ago, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court objected to search filters that let intelligence analysts pull Americans’ messages from intercepted data without the approvals, written justifications, or records the law requires. The court approved another year of surveillance anyway. The ruling has never been made public, and Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Adam Schiff of California say the administration’s own deadline for releasing it passed in September.

The program, Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), lapsed in June after Congress failed to renew it, though collection continues under the court’s March approval. The administration’s own public documentation says rulings like this one are reviewed for public release “within 180 days of issuance.” That window closed September 13, even as intelligence officials press lawmakers to reauthorize the program by the end of the year.

Wyden, the longest-serving member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, and Schiff, the former chair of its House counterpart, say the administration owes Congress an explanation for the delay, and the names of the officials responsible, by November 6.

“If this administration won’t follow this simple statutory directive,” the senators told Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Attorney General Todd Blanche in a demand letter obtained exclusively by WIRED, “it is unclear why Congress or the American people should trust this administration to follow any of the other legal limits to Section 702.”

Outside Congress, Demand Progress and 22 other civil liberties and government accountability groups on Monday urged congressional leaders to refuse to reauthorize Section 702 “while the administration actively withholds legally mandated information about how the surveillance program operates.” Signatories range from the American Civil Liberties Union to the conservative-backed Project for Privacy and Surveillance Accountability.

The Trump administration has already been pressed, and has promised, to release the ruling. In April, senators Tom Cotton and Mark Warner, the Intelligence Committee’s Republican chair and Democratic vice chair, pressed the administration to release it within 15 days so it could inform the Senate’s debate. In July, asked in writing whether he would commit to declassifying it by the 180-day deadline, Blanche replied, “Yes.”

Warner “has been clear that he supports transparency with regard to Section 702,” his communications director, Rachel Cohen, tells WIRED. Neither former director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard nor Bill Pulte, who briefly replaced her as acting director, “were responsive,” Cohen says, “but Senator Warner expects that DNI Clayton will declassify the opinion, consistent with the bipartisan letter and as required by law.”

Cotton’s office did not respond to a request for comment. The White House, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and the US Justice Department did not answer questions WIRED sent Friday about the delay.

Clayton, who is legally responsible as director of national intelligence for declassifying the ruling, has made no such promise. Asked before his July confirmation whether he would ensure the opinion was public before Congress voted on reauthorization, he wrote only that the government was “working arduously to expeditiously declassify” it and had made the full opinion available to lawmakers.

Some of what the court found is already known. A FISA court opinion declassified last year described a similar FBI tool, a “participants filter” that let agents select people in contact with surveillance targets and read their messages. In February 2025, the Justice Department’s National Security Division told the court the tool had been running searches no one counted. The FBI shut it off the next month and switched it back on later that year, after the department approved a rebuilt version.

This year’s ruling went beyond that. The court found that tools agencies use to narrow intercepted data to an American’s messages amount to searches of Americans, subject to the same limits, and ordered them rebuilt, The New York Times reported in April, citing unclassified administration talking points sent to lawmakers. Senator Alex Padilla said in a written question to Blanche that the Justice Department “is appealing portions” of the ruling “limiting the government’s use of certain filtering tools.”

While the ruling stayed secret, seven intelligence agency fact sheets from March 2026, one dated the day of the ruling, cited a 98.9 percent compliance rate for FBI searches of Americans and credited Section 702 with stopping a planned terrorist attack on a Taylor Swift concert in Vienna. None mentions the court’s findings. The figure appears nowhere in the Justice Department inspector general’s October 2025 review of those searches, which put the compliance rate at 98.6 percent and could not conclude that “the FBI’s querying compliance issues are entirely in the past.”

According to the fact sheets, FBI auditors review every such search. FBI director Kash Patel closed the bureau’s Office of Internal Auditing last May and moved its auditors into another division. The bureau’s search counts before 2025 also omit queries run through the participants filter, searches the government’s own privacy watchdog says are “not possible to track.”

Lawmakers who have read the ruling hint that it says more. Senator Dick Durbin, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, urged colleagues on the Senate floor in June to read it in a secure room. “I have seen it,” he said. Once they did, he told them, “your opinion of the role of FISA and the rights of Americans will be impacted for sure.”

Wyden has also warned about a classified interpretation of Section 702 that he says multiple administrations have relied on and refused to declassify. “When it is eventually declassified,” he said in March, “the American people are going to be stunned that it took so long and that Congress had been debating this authority with insufficient information.”

The Trump administration has until November 6 to answer the senators. The court’s current approval of the program expires in March.

Surveillance reform advocates say the administration may try to avoid that fight by attaching a renewal to the annual defense authorization bill, which Congress usually finalizes in December. In 2023, lawmakers extended Section 702 for four months through that year’s defense bill after a Senate effort to strip the provision failed. This year’s House and Senate versions of the bill do not yet include it.

items.article_content_zh:
两名长期监督美国情报的民主党参议员表示，特朗普政府非法向国会隐瞒秘密法庭的调查结果，直到立法者更新一项允许联邦特工在没有搜查令的情况下读取美国人通讯的计划。

七个月前，外国情报监视法院反对搜索过滤器，让情报分析人员在没有法律要求的批准、书面理由或记录的情况下从截获的数据中提取美国人的信息。不管怎样，法院还是批准了再监视一年。该裁决从未公开过，俄勒冈州参议员罗恩·怀登 (Ron Wyden) 和加利福尼亚州参议员亚当·希夫 (Adam Schiff) 表示，政府自己设定的公布裁决的最后期限已于 9 月份过去。

该计划属于《外国情报监视法》(FISA) 第 702 条，由于国会未能续签该计划，该计划于 6 月失效，不过在 3 月份法院批准后，收集工作仍在继续。政府自己的公开文件称，此类裁决将在“发布后 180 天内”进行审查并公开发布。尽管情报官员敦促立法者在年底前重新授权该计划，但该窗口已于 9 月 13 日关闭。

参议院情报委员会任职时间最长的成员怀登和众议院情报委员会前主席希夫表示，政府应在 11 月 6 日之前对国会的延误作出解释，并列出负责官员的姓名。

在《连线》杂志独家获得的一封要求信中，参议员们对国家情报总监杰伊·克莱顿和司法部长托德·布兰奇表示：“如果本届政府不遵守这一简单的法定指令，我们就不清楚为什么国会或美国人民应该相信本届政府会遵守第 702 条的任何其他法律限制。”

在国会之外，Demand Progress 和其他 22 个公民自由和政府问责组织周一敦促国会领导人拒绝重新授权第 702 条，“同时政府积极隐瞒有关监控计划如何运作的法定信息”。签署方包括美国公民自由联盟和保守派支持的隐私和监视问责项目。

特朗普政府已经受到压力，并承诺公布这一裁决。 4 月，参议员汤姆·科顿 (Tom Cotton) 和情报委员会共和党主席兼民主党副主席马克·沃纳 (Mark Warner) 敦促政府在 15 天内公布该报告，以便为参议院的辩论提供信息。 7 月份，当被问及是否会承诺在 180 天的期限内解密时，布兰奇回答说：“是的。”

华纳“已经明确表示，他支持第 702 条的透明度”，他的通讯总监雷切尔·科恩 (Rachel Cohen) 告诉《连线》杂志。前国家情报总监图尔西·加巴德（Tulsi Gabbard）和曾短暂取代她担任代理总监的比尔·普尔特（Bill Pulte）“都没有做出回应，”科恩说，“但华纳参议员预计国家情报总监克莱顿将根据两党信函并按照法律要求解密该意见。”

科顿的办公室没有回应置评请求。白宫、国家情报总监办公室和美国司法部没有回答《连线》杂志周五发出的有关延误的问题。

作为国家情报总监，克莱顿对解密该裁决负有法律责任，但他没有做出这样的承诺。在七月份的确认之前被问及是否会确保在国会就重新授权进行投票之前公开该意见时，他只写道，政府正在“努力迅速解密”该意见，并将完整的意见提供给立法者。

法院发现的一些内容已经为人所知。去年解密的 FISA 法庭意见描述了一种类似的 FBI 工具，即“参与者过滤器”，可以让特工选择与监视目标接触的人并阅读他们的消息。 2025 年 2 月，司法部国家安全部门告诉法庭，该工具一直在进行无人统计的搜索。联邦调查局在下个月将其关闭，并在该部门批准重建版本后于当年晚些时候将其重新打开。

今年的裁决超出了这一范围。据《纽约时报》四月份报道，法院援引发送给立法者的非机密政府谈话要点报道，法院发现，各机构用来将截获的数据缩小到美国人的信息范围的工具相当于对美国人的搜查，并受到同样的限制，并下令重建这些工具。参议员亚历克斯·帕迪拉在向布兰奇提出的书面问题中表示，司法部“正在对裁决中限制政府使用某些过滤工具的部分内容提出上诉”。

虽然该裁决仍然保密，但 2026 年 3 月的七份情报机构情况说明书（一份日期为裁决当天）指出，联邦调查局 (FBI) 对美国人的搜查遵守率为 98.9%，并称赞第 702 条阻止了针对泰勒·斯威夫特 (Taylor Swift) 维也纳演唱会策划的恐怖袭击。没有人提及法院的调查结果。这个数字在司法部监察长 2025 年 10 月对这些搜查的审查中没有出现，该审查得出的合规率为 98.6%，并且无法得出“FBI 询问合规问题完全是过去的事情”的结论。

根据情况说明书，联邦调查局审计员会审查每一次此类搜查。联邦调查局局长卡什·帕特尔去年五月关闭了该局的内部审计办公室，并将审计员转移到另一个部门。该局 2025 年之前的搜索计数也忽略了通过参与者过滤器进行的查询，政府自己的隐私监管机构称这些搜索“无法追踪”。

读过裁决的立法者暗示，它说了更多。司法委员会民主党领袖、参议员迪克·德宾 (Dick Durbin) 6 月份敦促参议院的同事在安全的房间里阅读该报告。 “我已经看到了，”他说。他告诉他们，一旦他们这样做，“你们对 FISA 作用和美国人权利的看法肯定会受到影响。”

怀登还对第 702 条的机密解释发出了警告，他说多个政府都依赖该解释并拒绝解密。 “当它最终解密时，”他在三月份表示，“美国人民将会感到震惊，因为它花了这么长时间，而且国会一直在信息不足的情况下就这一权威展开辩论。”

特朗普政府必须在 11 月 6 日之前对参议员做出答复。法院目前对该计划的批准将于三月份到期。

监视改革倡导者表示，政府可能会通过对年度国防授权法案进行更新来避免这场斗争，国会通常在 12 月最终确定该法案。 2023 年，在参议院废除第 702 条的努力失败后，立法者将第 702 条在当年的国防法案中延长了四个月。今年众议院和参议院版本的该法案尚未包含该内容。
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】民主党参议员怀登与希夫，以及美国情报行政部门在美国国会山与外国情报监视法院(FISC：扣押一份揭露非法监听手段的机密裁决，逾期拒绝向国会披露
【起因与机理】利用信息不对称，在《涉外情报监视法》第702条款面临到期续约的关键节点，掩盖情报机构的越权行为
【关键数据与实测】该裁决揭露了情报分析员非法利用搜索过滤器读取美国公民通信的违规操作，但政府为能在法案到期后强行续约，选择无视180天的公开披露期限强行锁死相关证据。
【观点态度】试图通过压制信息诱导法案续期。

[Root Cause & Mechanism] To manipulate the reauthorization process of Section 702 of the FISA, bypassing oversight on intelligence abuses
[Key Specification] Intelligence agency withholds secret court ruling.
[Perspective & Impact] Manipulating information to force legislative reauthorization.

items.title:
We don't just need smarter models, we need AI agents that are actually useful in everyday conversations.

I think @carte
items.title_en:
We don't just need smarter models, we need AI agents that are actually useful in everyday conversations.

I think @cartesia has got it right here. I've been testing out its new Managed Agents platform and it brings everything I need to make a voice agent into one stack: speech recognition, voice generation, the brains, interruptions and phone calls.

You choose your LLM, give the agent instructions, connect your tools, and Cartesia handles the rest. You can even build agents that answer customer questions, book appointments, or interact with users in different languages.

What I find interesting is how much infrastructure this removes for developers.

We've seen plenty of impressive voice AI demos, but getting them to work reliably in production is a different challenge.

I think making that process simpler is where the real opportunity lies.

Explore: https://t.co/Wk7SCAtxCQ

我认为让这个过程变得更简单才是真正的机会所在。

Teaching EKGs in the era of AI

Since the launch of Opus 5.5, there have been really cool e
items.title_en:
🚨 SOMETHING VERY DIFFERENT🚨

Teaching EKGs in the era of AI

Since the launch of Opus 5.5, there have been really cool examples of motion FX explainers teaching topics both simple and complex. I was seriously astounded by how good AI has gotten at building out visually stunning tools to teach and disseminate knowledge. I feel like it's a 1000x-er in how we approach education.

As an experiment for myself I tried to build a similar interactive-explainer I had seen on X for the specific topic of teaching EKGs, the workhorse of peering into the electrical activity of the heart. The premise was to create tutorials with motion, rather than slide decks.  Claude Opus 5.5 via the Claude Code harness was used to build something I would have actually wanted as an intern.

The Heart in Twelve Leads (Claude picked the name) is a 27-chapter interactive EKG atlas. Every tracing on the site is simulated from one 3D heart: an activation wave crosses the muscle, electrical currents sum to a heart vector based on biophysical principles, and each of the twelve leads records that vector and applies it to the model.

It starts with the basics: what are leads, and how do leads actually pick up electrical activity. It helps orient lead placement to rhythm strips so you can visually see the relationship between the two, something that always confused me in medical school.

The model can map pathology, such as bundle branch block, ischemia, alterations in electrolytes, and arrhythmias. It pairs lead readings with a dynamic model of the heart showing electrical movement down conduction paths, so you can map the raw electrical activity with what the EKG sees.

Each disease is a change to that same underlying biophysical model of the heart, so the leads stay consistent with each other and with the anatomy.

I was inspired by the incredible echocardiogram teaching site built by @David_Ouyang’s intro2echo lab (https://t.co/OoXhTJmQAI). His echo simulator made me want the ECG version (more relevant to what I have to think about in psychiatry). The goal is to actually sit inside the physiology instead of memorizing pattern lists. Huge shoutout for helping me think "bigger", which is still the bottleneck IMO in getting physicians to fully embrace AI.

This is a VERY VERY VERY preliminary site. I have not fact checked anything, and instead wanted to see the capacity of Claude to "one-shot" production. I had probably 10 prompts of steering/approvals, but ultimately I accepted everything with minimal amount of human intervention.

What we can do today as humans with the help of @claudeai or other frontier models is truly mesmerizing. If this is something you would want to build upon and bring to life, let me know!

Site: https://t.co/vCyyZ5WILR

I was seriously astounded by how good AI has gotten at building out visually stunning tools to teach and disseminate knowledge. I feel like it's a 1000x-er in how we approach education.

As an experiment for myself I tried to build a similar interactive-explainer I had seen on X for the specific topic of teaching EKGs, the workhorse of peering into the electrical activity of the heart. The Heart in Twelve Leads (Claude picked the name) is a 27-chapter interactive EKG atlas. Every tracing on the site is simulated from one 3D heart: an activation wave crosses the muscle, electrical currents sum to a heart vector based on biophysical principles, and each of the twelve leads records that vector and applies it to the model.

items.title_en:
All my life I was terrified someone watching me through laptop camera, even the FBI director taped his...

Claude Code dug through my laptop's hidden logs and found suspicious moments I can't explain 

check yours and shut down your camera without a sticker:

what it found:

- an unknown app turning on my camera at night, while I sleep
- Windows quietly remembers apps (could be spy) that turned on your camera, even after you delete them

why you should do it today:

- a $40 spy tool bought in 100+ countries infected 500,000+ computers and could switch on their webcams remotely (US Departament of Justice)
- a US school district secretly took 30,000+ webcam photos of students on school laptops, some inside their homes (Lower Merion)
- even FBI director put tape over his laptop camera (James Comey)

Windows:

1. install repo below and type /camera-guard in Claude Code, it reads the hidden log of every app that ever turned on your camera and mic

2. delete AnyDesk, TeamViewer ot any remote app you don't use

3. Windows has a hidden "Camera on/off pop-up, off by default, ask Claude to turn it on and you see every time the camera starts

4. really shut camera off, Settings switch isn't enough:

• BIOS (strongest ): hold shift, click Restart - Troubleshoot → Advancedf options → UEFI Firmware Settings , set Camera to Disabled and add a BIOS password.

Windows can't see the camera at all. Need it for a call? - Turn it back on there. Not every laptop has it, Claude checks your model

• camera switch or key: some laptops have a slider on the side or an F-key with a crossed-out camera. Slide it off when you're not using it

• Device Manager → Cameras → Desible device: one click to undo (but any app with admin rights can undo it too)

5. run Microsoft Defender Offline, the deep scan built into Windows (Windows Security → Virus & threat protection → scan options): it restarts your PC and hunts hard-to-catch spyware before Windows starts

Mac: 

1. install repo below and type /camera-guard, it checks which apps can use your camera and mic and what starts with your Mac

2. System Settings → General → Sharing: turn off Screen Sharing, Remote Login and Remote Management, these let someone see and control your Mac from another computer

3. Screen Time → Content & Privacy → App & Feature Restrictions → Camera: off + a Screen time passcode - Apple's own camera off swith

4. install OverSight, free Mac app: it pops up an alert second any app turns on your camera or mic, so you know the moment anyhting starts filming or listening

items.title: Holy Shit: WIRED reports an Accenture contractor gave a Claude Code agent admin access to NIPRNet, an unclassified Penta
items.title_en:
Holy Shit: WIRED reports an Accenture contractor gave a Claude Code agent admin access to NIPRNet, an unclassified Pentagon network, to write and deploy code. It ran for two months, apparently sending login credentials, passwords and a network map to a third-party site NIST had flagged as high risk.

Contractors must report breaches within 72 hours, yet sources say Accenture initially didn't report it at all. A source calls it "100 percent a national security threat."
items.title_zh: 天哪：《连线》报道称，埃森哲承包商向 Claude Code 代理授予了 NIPRNet（一个非机密五角大楼网络）的管理员访问权限，以编写和部署代码。它运行了两个月，显然将登录凭据、密码和网络地图发送到 NIST 标记为高风险的第三方网站。

I can only imagine the poor Accenture compliance officer when they learned out it. Shadow AI is a compliance nightmare.

我真的很纠结哪个更糟糕：承包商在国防部网络上运行个人人工智能代理，或者国防部花了很长时间才弄清楚这一点。

我只能想象可怜的埃森哲合规官员得知此事后的情景。影子人工智能是一场合规噩梦。

items.title_en:
closed source is dead...

i just reverse-engineered CCleaner / CleanMyMac with Opus 5.5 for Mac & Windows PC

$40/year cleaners → replaced in one afternoon.

→ https://t.co/O2rv5UuR8b

free. open code. no account. no upsells.

how it came together:

• step 1 → Claude Code on Opus 5.5 in an empty folder. one long prompt + a few CleanMyMac screenshots

• step 2 → no code at first. Opus mocked up 9 different designs, i picked the one i liked and it kept polishing

• step 3 → 8 agents worked at the same time, each on its own part:

scanner, disk map, AI, startup apps, installers

• step 4 → the rule that makes it safe: caches get deleted (they come back on their own), anything you made goes to the Trash first

• step 5 → one more agent’s only job was to break it.

it found a sneaky Windows path that could’ve trashed my entire Documents folder. fixed before i ever pressed Clean

• step 6 → first click on my own PC: 14.6 GB freed

• step 7 → ask the built-in AI (Claude or ChatGPT) “what can i delete?”

it sees file names and sizes, never what’s inside them

• step 8 → GitHub builds the Mac and Windows installers on every release. i never touched a Mac

paid cleaners charge you to delete your own cache.
this one shows you the code.

Find full prompt below ↓

Then read the article on how to Reverse Engineer Anything with Opus 5.5.
